glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The main point is that believers have a High Priest seated in heaven who ministers in the true tabernacle and mediates the better covenant God promised through Jeremiah, in which He writes His laws on His people’s hearts, makes Himself known to all of them, and remembers their sins no more.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Hebrews 8 gathers up the priesthood argument of chapter 7 and moves it into God’s presence. It quotes Jeremiah 31:31–34 in full and prepares for the explanation of Christ’s sacrifice in chapters 9 and 10.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the LORD: I will put My laws in their mind and write them on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people.” (Hebrews 8:10)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
After seven chapters of argument, Hebrews pauses to state its main point: “We have such a High Priest” (8:1). He is seated at God’s right hand, serving in “the true tabernacle which the Lord erected, and not man” (8:2). The tabernacle Moses built was God-given and true to its pattern, but it was “the copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (8:5). Jesus ministers in the reality those copies pictured.

His ministry is greater because the covenant He mediates is greater, “a better covenant, which was established on better promises” (8:6). God Himself announced it through Jeremiah, finding fault with a people who “did not continue in My covenant” (8:9). The new covenant answers what the old could not. God will put His laws in His people’s minds and write them on their hearts. He will be their God, and they will be His people. All of them, “from the least of them to the greatest of them,” will know Him personally, and He will remember their sins and lawless deeds no more (8:10–12).

By calling this covenant new, God has made the first one obsolete, and what is growing old “is ready to vanish away” (8:13). The chapter leaves the reader standing before a High Priest who is already serving in heaven and already bringing His people into the covenant God promised.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Hebrews 8:1–5 — The Main Point: A High Priest in the Heavens

The main point of everything said so far is that believers have a High Priest seated at God’s right hand, serving in the true tabernacle the Lord Himself set up. Earthly priests served a copy and shadow of heavenly realities, made by the pattern God showed Moses.

Hebrews 8:6–7 — Mediator of a Better Covenant

Jesus’ ministry is greater because He mediates a better covenant founded on better promises. If the first covenant had been without fault, there would have been no need for a second.

Hebrews 8:8–12 — God’s Promise of a New Covenant

Finding fault with His people, God promised through Jeremiah a new covenant with Israel and Judah, unlike the one their fathers broke after the exodus. In it He writes His laws on their hearts, makes Himself known to all of them, and forgives their sins completely.

Hebrews 8:13 — The First Covenant Made Obsolete

By calling the covenant new, God declared the first covenant obsolete. What is aging and growing old is ready to disappear.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Hebrews 8 shows that the gospel brings an inward change God Himself performs. Under the new covenant God does not only command His people from outside; He writes His laws on their hearts and makes Himself personally known to every one of them (8:10–11). Obedience grows out of what God does within.

The chapter also grounds believers’ confidence in forgiveness. God promises to remember their sins no more (8:12), and Jesus, the Mediator of that promise, is already serving in heaven. Every believer, from the least to the greatest, can know God and draw near through Him.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The main point. Believers have a High Priest seated in heaven (8:1).

Copy and reality. The earthly tabernacle was a God-given copy of the heavenly sanctuary where Jesus serves (8:2–5).

A better covenant. Jesus mediates a covenant established on better promises (8:6–7).

Hearts made new. God writes His laws within His people and makes Himself known to all of them (8:10–11).

Sins remembered no more. Full forgiveness lies at the heart of the new covenant (8:12).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The true tabernacle (8:2). The heavenly reality of God’s dwelling, which the Lord Himself set up. Jesus ministers there.

Copy and shadow (8:5). The earthly tabernacle was real and God-given, but it pictured something greater. God told Moses to build it according to the pattern shown him on the mountain (Exodus 25:40).

Mediator (8:6). One who stands between two parties to establish and maintain their relationship. Jesus brings His people into the new covenant and keeps them in it.

New covenant (8:8). The covenant God promised through Jeremiah to the house of Israel and the house of Judah (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus mediates it, bringing its promises of inward change, knowledge of God, and forgiveness to His people.

“All shall know Me” (8:11). Every member of the new covenant knows God personally. Teaching still helps believers grow in that knowledge, which will reach its fullness when Christ returns (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Obsolete (8:13). No longer in force. Hebrews applies the word to the Sinai covenant and its priestly order, which give way to the new covenant.

focus: Hebrews 8 states the main point of the argument: believers have a High Priest seated in heaven who ministers in the true tabernacle, of which the earthly sanctuary was only a copy and shadow. His more excellent ministry rests on the better covenant God promised through Jeremiah, in which He writes His laws on hearts, makes Himself known to all His people, and forgives their sins, making the first covenant obsolete.

sections.title: The Main Point: A High Priest in the Heavens
sections.summary: “Now this is the main point of the things we are saying: We have such a High Priest” (Hebrews 8:1), seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens and ministering in the true tabernacle which the Lord erected. The earthly priests serve “the copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), made according to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain.

sections.title: Mediator of a Better Covenant
sections.summary: Jesus has obtained a more excellent ministry because He is Mediator of “a better covenant, which was established on better promises” (Hebrews 8:6). If the first covenant had been faultless, no place would have been sought for a second.

sections.title: God’s Promise of a New Covenant
sections.summary: Finding fault with the people, God announced through Jeremiah a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah, unlike the covenant their fathers did not continue in after He led them out of Egypt. In it God will put His laws in their mind and write them on their hearts, be their God, cause all of them to know Him from the least to the greatest, and remember their sins and lawless deeds no more.

sections.title: The First Covenant Made Obsolete
sections.summary: By speaking of “A new covenant” (Hebrews 8:13), God has made the first obsolete. What is becoming obsolete and growing old “is ready to vanish away” (Hebrews 8:13).

1.brief: “Now this is the main point of the things we are saying: We have such a High Priest,” one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens. Everything said about Jesus’ priesthood comes to this: believers have Him now, enthroned beside God.
1.explain: “We have such a High Priest” The priest just described in Hebrews 7 is the priest the congregation has now. He is seated in the heavens at the right hand of God’s throne, where His royal authority and priestly service meet. Hebrews calls this the main point because the better priest gives His people a real relationship to God’s presence.

2.brief: Jesus serves as “a Minister of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle which the Lord erected, and not man.” His ministry takes place in the real dwelling of God, which the Lord Himself established.
2.explain: “a Minister of the sanctuary” Jesus actively serves in the true tabernacle. The Lord Himself established that sanctuary. Its reality explains why the earthly sanctuary, though given by God, could serve as a copy.

3.brief: Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices, so this High Priest must also have something to offer. Hebrews prepares to explain what Jesus offered, which chapters 9 and 10 make plain.
3.explain: “this One also have something to offer” Offering gifts and sacrifices belongs to the assignment of every high priest. That established pattern raises the question of Jesus’ offering. Hebrews 9:24–28 answers it by joining His once-for-all sacrifice to His present appearance before God for us.

4.brief: If Jesus were on earth, He would not be a priest at all, since priests already offer the gifts the law requires. His priesthood does not belong to the earthly order of the law but to heaven.
4.explain: “if He were on earth” The existing earthly priests offer the prescribed gifts under the law. Jesus comes from Judah, so He would hold no priestly place under those provisions. His ministry takes place in God’s presence under a different appointment.

5.brief: The earthly priests serve “the copy and shadow of the heavenly things,” as Moses was told when he was about to build the tabernacle: “See that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.” The tabernacle was God-given and true, yet it was a copy of the heavenly reality where Jesus now ministers.
5.explain: “the copy and shadow of the heavenly things” Moses was told in Exodus 25:40 to build according to what God showed him on the mountain. The instruction gives the earthly tabernacle its authority and shows its limits. Its carefully ordered service points beyond itself to the heavenly sanctuary in which Jesus ministers.

6.brief: Jesus has now obtained a more excellent ministry, because He is also Mediator of “a better covenant, which was established on better promises.” From the heavenly sanctuary He brings His people into the better covenant God promised, with the inward change, personal knowledge of God, and forgiveness that the chapter goes on to name.
6.explain: “Mediator of a better covenant” Jesus has received the more excellent ministry because He brings His people into the better covenant. The better promises that underlie it are the ones Jeremiah will name: God works within His people, gives them knowledge of Himself, and remembers their sins no more. Through Jesus those promises are already at work.

7.brief: “For if that first covenant had been faultless, then no place would have been sought for a second.” The need for a second covenant shows the limits of the first, which did not bring the better promises God names in Hebrews 8:8–12: His laws written on the heart, every member knowing Him, and sins remembered no more.
7.explain: “no place would have been sought for a second” God’s announcement of another covenant shows the limits of the first. What the first covenant required, Jeremiah’s promise goes on to describe God bringing about within His people. Hebrews will also show why a new priestly offering is necessary for complete forgiveness.

8.brief: Finding fault with the people, God announced through Jeremiah, “Behold, the days are coming, says the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.” The new covenant is God’s own initiative, promised to His people Israel and Judah.
8.explain: “with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” God finds fault with the people and announces through Jeremiah a new covenant with the two houses named in the promise. Their unfaithfulness explains the setting of the promise. Hebrews quotes it to explain what Jesus now mediates.

9.brief: The new covenant would not be like the one God made with their fathers when He led them out of Egypt, “because they did not continue in My covenant, and I disregarded them, says the LORD.” Israel’s failure to remain faithful exposed the limits of the first covenant.
9.explain: “they did not continue in My covenant” God recalls taking the ancestors by the hand to bring them out of Egypt. That care makes their failure to remain faithful especially plain. His statement that He disregarded them describes His response to their breach and shows why the new covenant has to differ.

10.brief: In the covenant God will make, He promises, “I will put My laws in their mind and write them on their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be My people.” God Himself will work inwardly, changing His people’s hearts and binding them to Himself.
10.explain: “I will put My laws in their mind and write them on their hearts” God takes the initiative to place His instruction within His people. The mind comes to understand what pleases Him, and the heart is moved to obey. God’s pledge to be their God names the relationship this inward work serves.

11.brief: Through Jesus every member of the new covenant already knows the Lord personally, so no one needs to tell his neighbor, “Know the LORD,” for “all shall know Me, from the least of them to the greatest of them.” Christian teaching still helps believers grow in knowing the God they already know, and that knowledge awaits its fullness when Christ returns.
11.explain: “all shall know Me” Through Jesus every member of the new covenant knows God personally, from the least to the greatest. In Israel a person could belong outwardly and still need the call to know the Lord. Christian teachers help believers grow in knowing the God they already know. The promise is at work now and will reach its fullness when Christ returns.

12.brief: God promises, “For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness, and their sins and their lawless deeds I will remember no more.” At the heart of the new covenant is God’s full and lasting forgiveness.
12.explain: “I will remember no more” God pledges mercy for wrongdoing and forgiveness for sins and lawless deeds. Remembering their sins no more means He will no longer hold them against His people. Hebrews 10:14–18 joins that promise to Jesus’ single offering.

13.brief: By calling this covenant new, God “has made the first obsolete,” and what is becoming obsolete and growing old “is ready to vanish away.” The first covenant and its priestly order give way to the new covenant Jesus mediates.
13.explain: “He has made the first obsolete” By calling the covenant new God marks the earlier Sinai covenant and its priestly order as old. Growing old and being ready to vanish picture an order giving way to the covenant Jesus already mediates. Chapter 9 explains the earlier sanctuary and rites with that change in view.
